plain: In late 2001, at Tora Bora in the mountains of Afghanistan, an American special forces commander known as Dalton Fury is said to have had Osama bin Laden within reach and been kept from going after him. John Blitch, a former scientist at DARPA, the Pentagon's advanced research agency, tells Michels what Fury said: that Fury went on 60 Minutes in disguise and told the correspondent Scott Pelley he had had "Direct OverWatch" on bin Laden, meaning he could watch and strike him, "on three separate occasions". Blitch also points to Fury's book Kill Bin Laden. The 60 Minutes report itself, broadcast on October 5, 2008, tells it somewhat differently. In it Fury says two plans from his unit, Delta, were turned down from above: one to come over the mountains from the Pakistan side, and one to mine the passes into Pakistan. Pelley reports that they "didn't get approval from a higher level" and that the second plan "was also disapproved", and that "the military wouldn't tell 60 Minutes who rejected the plans or why." The report does not speak of having bin Laden in sight three times or of overwatch. On the night his team was "about 2,000 meters away from where we think bin Laden's at", the report has Fury himself deciding not to push on, saying "it wasn't worth the risk at that particular moment to go up there and play cowboy." If Blitch's version is right, it would mean the man behind 9/11 was spared by a decision made higher up.

discussion.by: Elite Officer Recalls Bin Laden Hunt (60 Minutes)
discussion.text: In the 60 Minutes report of October 2008, Dalton Fury says two of Delta's plans against bin Laden at Tora Bora (coming over the mountains from the Pakistan side, and mining the passes into Pakistan) were disapproved by higher headquarters; the report does not speak of having bin Laden in sight three times or of overwatch, and it says that on the night his team was about 2,000 meters from where they thought bin Laden was, Fury himself decided not to advance.
